newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK C.BANK PLANS TO LOWER INTERBANK RATES - GOVT.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK C.BANK PLANS TO LOWER INTERBANK RATES - GOVT.

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) plans to lower and stabilise interest rates on the country's interbank money market, a government spokeswoman said on Tuesday.

"(Central bank) Governor Vladimir Masar has proposed certain measures to lower and stabilise interest rates on the interbank money market," government spokeswoman Magda Pospisilova said after a regular government meeting where Masar was in attendance.
Pospisilova said the unspecified measures had been proposed at a meeting between the country's leading bankers, the NBS and Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar last Saturday. She gave no further details.
When contacted for details, NBS press officials said they were not informed about the plan.
Money market rates jumped to record levels in the first weeks of January, after the NBS moved to rein in a rapidly growing money supply and cool off a consumption-led boom.

The latest NBS move to hold securities repurchase tenders instead of quoting repo rates -- which many domestic banks often used to refinance their activities -- brought an acute liquidity shortage on the interbank market at the beginning of the year, pushing rates to around 27 percent.
Rates have since retreated, ranging on Tuesday between 19.6/20.4 percent on overnight money to 17.5/18.0 percent for six-month funds.

Last week Finance Minister Sergej Kozlik sharply criticised the central bank's restrictive monetary policy, saying it could hurt the entire economy. He said NBS attempts to rapidly reduce money supply growth were inappropriate.

"The situation on the interbank market, where interest rates are exceeding inflation by more than three times, was not caused by the government, but by the excessive restrictive monetary policy of the NBS," Kozlik said.
Money market dealers said they did not expect significant rate fluctuations in the near future.
"We think the NBS wants to keep rates above 18 percent and no significant jumps or falls are expected in coming days," Patrik Banary of Slovenska Sporitelna told Reuters.
